title_options: Chilli Never Actually Heats Your Mouth 🌶️

share.myth: Chilli burns because it is hot or is actually damaging your mouth.
share.truth: Capsaicin opens TRPV1, the nerve sensor that normally fires at about 43 degrees Celsius, so the brain reads burning heat with no real rise in temperature (Caterina et al. 1997).
share.line: Chilli doesn't heat your mouth. It switches on the sensor that warns you about burning heat.

facts: Caterina MJ et al. 1997, Nature 389:816-824: the capsaicin receptor VR1 (now TRPV1) is an ion channel on pain nerves that is also opened by heat in the painful range; its threshold is about 43 C (Caterina 1999 Nature; reviews).
David Julius shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering receptors for temperature and touch, starting with the capsaicin receptor TRPV1.

Nolden, Lenart & Hayes 2019, Physiology & Behavior: of the drinks tested, whole and skim milk reduced capsaicin burn the most; skim worked about as well as whole, pointing to protein, not only fat; carbonated drinks did least.
description: Chilli never raises the temperature in your mouth. Its molecule, capsaicin, opens TRPV1, the nerve sensor that normally fires at about 43 °C, so your brain hears a heat alarm. #shorts #science #biology #chilli
sources: Caterina et al. 1997, Nature 389:816 (the capsaicin receptor, a heat-activated ion channel); Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2021 (nobelprize.org); Nolden, Lenart & Hayes 2019, Physiology & Behavior (milk and oral burn).

scenes.narration: Chilli never actually heats your mouth. Your tongue just thinks it's on fire.
The nerves in your tongue carry a tiny sensor called TRPV1. Its job is to warn you about burning heat.
At about forty-three degrees Celsius, around a hundred and nine Fahrenheit, it springs open, and your brain hears: hot!
The molecule in chilli, called capsaicin, slots into the very same sensor and opens it, with no heat at all.
So your brain gets the same alarm, and you sweat and go red, as if you really were hot.
Finding this sensor won the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
And in a taste test, milk calmed the burn best. Even skim milk.
So chilli doesn't heat your mouth. It switches on the sensor that warns you about burning heat.
